situations.title: I feel like I'm panicking
situations.subtitle: Palpitations, rapid breathing, dizziness, or feeling out of control
situations.immediateExplanation: The body's alarm system may have activated too loudly. The sensations are real, although by themselves they do not allow us to know if it is panic or another problem.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your body is not inventing these sensations: it is very strongly activating a protection system. When the brain's alarm networks interpret that there is danger, the sympathetic nervous system prepares muscles, heart and lungs to defend or escape. Messengers such as adrenaline and norepinephrine help the heart beat faster, increase alertness, and tense the body. It's a useful response to a real threat, but it can feel terrifying when activated without clear danger.

If you start breathing too fast, you eliminate more carbon dioxide than usual. That change can contribute to dizziness, tingling, tightness, or a feeling of unreality; The sensations feed fear and fear accelerates breathing even more. What you think is happening also influences how the brain interprets each body signal, although that does not make the symptoms imaginary.

Orienting yourself to safe data in the present and letting the exhale be gentle brings in new information: “Right now I can stop and observe.” With practice, the brain can learn that these intense sensations do not always herald catastrophe. If they are new, different or very intense, a medical cause must first be ruled out.
situations.reassurance: You don't need to fight every sensation. Check that you are safe first and let the body gradually reduce activation.
redFlags: It is the first time that you have severe chest pain or symptoms that you do not recognize.
Symptoms began during physical exertion or together with an allergic reaction.
whenToSeekHelp: If the episodes repeat themselves, they condition your life or you begin to avoid places out of fear.
If you cannot distinguish these sensations from a medical problem.
If a breathing technique increases dizziness or a feeling of suffocation.

situations.title: I feel overwhelmed by work
situations.subtitle: Pressure, blockage, too many tasks, or difficulty thinking clearly
situations.immediateExplanation: Under pressure, attention can narrow and everything seems equally urgent. The first goal is not to solve everything, but to regain enough clarity to choose a single action.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
When you perceive too many demands and few resources to respond, your brain increases the priority of everything related to deadlines, errors and evaluation. Some job threats are social or anticipated, but they can still activate body stress systems. The sympathetic system mobilizes energy quickly and the stress hormone axis can sustain the response for longer. That's why you may notice tense jaw and shoulders, higher breathing, irritability or the feeling of having to do everything now.

In this state, attention is narrowed and working memory has less space. It is not that you have lost capacity: a part of your resources is busy monitoring problems, remembering pending issues and predicting consequences. If this pattern repeats, the body may begin to anticipate activation due to signals such as a notification, an email, or the start of the day.

A physical break and a single priority don't make the real load go away, but they reduce the simultaneous signals your brain must process. Repeating limits, breaks, and concrete actions can create a more flexible learned pattern: detect the demand, regulate yourself, and then respond, rather than continually staying in urgency mode.
situations.reassurance: Being saturated does not mean being incapable. Your brain may need less input and a concrete priority, not more pressure.
redFlags: You are driving, using machinery, or performing a task where losing attention can be dangerous.
whenToSeekHelp: If stress persists for weeks, it disrupts sleep or causes frequent physical symptoms.
If there is harassment, violence, threats or an unsafe work environment.
If you need harmful substances or behaviors to continue.

situations.title: My emotions feel too intense
situations.subtitle: Sadness, anguish or overload that occupies all the attention
situations.immediateExplanation: Intense emotion can take up much of your attention and make it difficult to think broadly. Giving it space does not mean obeying it or resigning yourself to feeling it forever.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
An intense emotion does not live only "in the head." It is a coordinated pattern between brain and body that organizes attention, retrieves related memories, changes internal sensations and prepares you to act. The closed chest, the heat, the knot in the stomach or the desire to cry are part of that response. Your brain receives these body signals and interprets them using context, your previous experiences, and what you expect to happen.

When activation increases a lot, the mind temporarily loses amplitude: it is difficult to maintain several ideas, consider nuances or imagine alternatives. The emotion seems to occupy all of reality because the stimuli related to it receive priority. That doesn't mean that the emotion is wrong or that you should obey every impulse it brings.

Naming what you notice and anchoring some of your attention in the present adds a little distance between feeling and acting. By repeating this sequence, you practice a regulation skill: the body can be activated and, at the same time, you can choose a safe behavior. Neuroplasticity is gradual; It does not erase emotions, but it allows you to learn new ways of relating to them.
situations.reassurance: Emotion is an experience that is occurring; It is not your entire identity nor an order that you must follow.
redFlags: The emotion is accompanied by a desire to disappear, hurt yourself, or stop being safe.
whenToSeekHelp: If the intensity lasts for days or interferes significantly with your life.
If thoughts of self-harm, intense hopelessness or increasing isolation appear.
If the emotion is related to violence, abuse, or a traumatic loss.

situations.title: I'm scared and I don't know what to do
situations.subtitle: Anticipated threat, insecurity or need to regain stability
situations.immediateExplanation: Fear prepares the body to protect you. Before trying to convince yourself that everything is fine, it is worth distinguishing whether there is a real danger and what part belongs to a prediction.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your protection system is designed to react quickly. Networks that detect threats prefer a false alarm to ignoring a real danger, so they can activate the body before you have analyzed the entire situation. The sympathetic system accelerates heart and breathing, directs attention to possible risks and prepares for fight or flight; Other protective responses can leave you immobile or blocked.

Fear also uses memory and prediction. If something resembles a difficult experience, the brain can fill in what's missing with the outcome it fears. Your expectations influence what signals you see and how you interpret body sensations, but they do not magically determine reality. That is why it is convenient to separate "what is happening" from "what my mind anticipates."

Looking around, checking security, and formulating a concrete plan provides current data to the nervous system. When you safely navigate a manageable situation, the brain can update its prediction and learn that there is more than one possible response. That learning needs repetition and must be done gradually; If there is real danger, protecting yourself and asking for help remains the priority.
situations.reassurance: You can respect the fear signal without letting it completely decide the next step.
redFlags: There is a violent person, a real threat, or a physically unsafe place. In that case, prioritize walking away and asking for help.
whenToSeekHelp: If the fear is related to violence, control or threats from another person.
If you increasingly avoid important activities or places.
If fear appears frequently and intensely without a clear cause.

situations.title: I can't stop thinking about it
situations.subtitle: Doubts, anticipation, checking or repetitive thoughts
situations.immediateExplanation: Thinking more does not always produce more certainty. When the mind tries to eliminate all uncertainty, it can repeat the same check without generating new information.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your mind is trying to achieve certainty and protect you from error. To do this, keep the problem active, rehearse scenarios, and review the same data again. The drawback is that working memory has limited capacity: the more space occupied by doubt, the less there is left to observe new information, rest or make a simple decision. That's why thinking for longer can cause fatigue without getting you closer to an answer.

Checking, reviewing, or asking for reassurance usually reduces anxiety for a few moments. That relief works as a reward and the brain learns: “when doubt arises, I should check again.” The cycle strengthens even if the intention is to feel safe. Furthermore, the more you look for absolute certainty, the more striking the small exceptions seem.

Saying “I am having the thought that…” is not intended to make it false; It helps to recognize it as a mental activity, not as an order. Returning later to an observable action teaches another route: I can tolerate some uncertainty and continue acting. Repetition does not eliminate all doubt, but it can weaken the habit of always responding with another check.
situations.reassurance: You don't need to resolve all the uncertainty to take a reasonable step.
redFlags: Thoughts order you to do harm, you feel like you are losing touch with reality, or you can't stay safe.
whenToSeekHelp: If thoughts consume a large part of the day or generate checks that are difficult to stop.
If they persistently affect sleep, work, or relationships.
If strange perceptual experiences or loss of contact with reality appear.

situations.title: I'm very angry or caught in a conflict
situations.subtitle: Impulse to respond, intense discussion, or difficulty stopping
situations.immediateExplanation: Anger can signal a limit, an injustice, or a need. With high arousal, responding immediately increases the risk of saying or doing something that complicates the conflict.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your body is activating its sympathetic nervous system and preparing you to defend yourself, set a limit, or move away an obstacle. Messengers such as adrenaline and norepinephrine increase alertness, speed up the heart and make it easier for muscles to tense. Breathing can become faster, hands close, and attention is almost automatically directed toward the provocation. It is not a breakdown: it is protective energy, although acting from its peak can worsen the conflict.

With a lot of activation, it is more difficult for the brain to stop an already prepared response and consider long-term consequences. Ambiguous words sound more hostile and it is easier to find evidence that the other person is completely wrong. A pause does not invalidate the limit or force forgiveness; it simply prevents physiology from deciding for you during the peak.

By creating distance, dropping objects, and moving harmlessly, you stop adding confrontation cues and allow time for the arousal to subside. Practicing this sequence can turn it into a learned response: noticing the anger, protecting safety, and then choosing how to express the need. If there is violence or you fear losing control, the priority is to get away and ask for help.
situations.reassurance: Pausing does not invalidate your limit. It helps you express it with more control.
redFlags: There are weapons, physical violence, threats or you are afraid of losing control and causing harm. Walk away and ask for immediate help.
whenToSeekHelp: If there is violence, threats, fear or control within the relationship.
If the outbursts are repeated or damage important relationships.
If you consume alcohol or other substances during conflicts.

situations.title: I can't sleep because of what has happened
situations.subtitle: The mind reviews the problem and the body remains alert
situations.immediateExplanation: After a hard day, trying to force yourself to sleep can increase alertness. The immediate objective is not to forcefully achieve sleep, but to create conditions of rest and reduce the struggle with insomnia.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Sleep depends on two processes working together: sleep pressure that builds up during awake time and the circadian clock that organizes when your body expects to sleep. Even when you are both prepared, a heightened internal alarm can keep you vigilant. If the brain interprets that there is still a problem to solve, it keeps attention, muscle tension and part of the stress response active.

Trying to force yourself to sleep adds a task that is impossible to execute at will. Looking at the time, calculating the remaining hours, and checking to see if “it's already working” teach the brain to associate bed with evaluation and effort. Every thought about the next day's consequences can raise another little red flag, even if you're exhausted.

Changing the goal from sleep to rest reduces that struggle. Low light, neutral activity, and temporarily getting out of bed when you are clearly awake help reconstruct the association between bed and sleepiness. Learning happens with repetition, not because one night turns out perfect. If insomnia persists or appears with other important symptoms, it requires professional evaluation.
situations.reassurance: A difficult night is exhausting, but you don't have to figure out your entire life now. You can dedicate this moment only to rest.
redFlags: You've had almost no sleep for several nights and you notice unusual energy, very fast thinking, confusion, or risky behavior.
Lack of sleep appears with severe pain, shortness of breath, substance withdrawal, or a reaction to medication.
whenToSeekHelp: If the problem lasts for months, recurs frequently or significantly affects your daily life.
If you snore with pauses in breathing, you fall asleep involuntarily or driving becomes unsafe.
If thoughts of harming yourself appear or you feel like you can't keep yourself safe.

protocols.title: Let go of the fight with sleep
protocols.summary: Change the goal of sleeping now to resting without solving problems tonight.
protocols.caution: Do not use your phone to complete the steps. If you need to get up, do so in dim light and avoiding stimulating activities.

steps.title: Hide the time
steps.instruction: Put the clock out of sight and stop calculating how much sleep you have left.
steps.accessibilityCue: Stop checking the time.

steps.title: Change the goal

steps.accessibilityCue: Allow yourself to rest without forcing sleep.

steps.title: Park the problem
steps.instruction: Summarize the concern in one sentence and decide on a specific time tomorrow to review it.
steps.accessibilityCue: Leave the problem for a specific time tomorrow.

steps.title: Choose neutrality
steps.instruction: Imagine a known route or list objects in a category without seeking to make it perfect.
steps.accessibilityCue: Bring attention to a neutral mental task.

steps.title: Calmly reassess
steps.instruction: If you're still clearly awake, get out of bed for a while and do something quiet in low light; Return when drowsiness appears.
steps.accessibilityCue: If you're still awake, choose a quiet activity outside of bed.

protocols.title: Neutral body tour
protocols.summary: Observe areas of the body without requiring them to relax or controlling their breathing.

steps.title: Seek support
steps.instruction: Notice where the bed supports your head, back, and legs.
steps.accessibilityCue: Notice the support points of your body.

steps.title: Face and jaw

steps.accessibilityCue: It runs through the trunk, legs and feet.

steps.instruction: Stop running through the body. Allow your breathing to continue on its own and return to a comfortable posture.

protocols.summary: Generate neutral and disconnected images to distance yourself from a story that is trying to resolve itself.

steps.title: Choose a letter

steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a letter.

steps.title: Imagine words
steps.instruction: Think of a neutral word with that letter, imagine it and change to another without creating a story.

steps.title: Leave it incomplete

steps.accessibilityCue: Allow it to remain incomplete.

practicalTips.title: Hide the time
practicalTips.detail: Turn your watch or phone so you don't turn every wake-up into a calculation.

practicalTips.title: Try a small thermal change
practicalTips.detail: Take one foot out of the blanket, switch sides of the pillow, or briefly ventilate.

practicalTips.title: Choose a familiar audio
practicalTips.detail: A familiar voice, with a timer and low volume, demands less attention than new content.

situations.title: A social situation blocks me
situations.subtitle: A meeting, event or conversation raises fear of being judged
situations.immediateExplanation: Social anxiety can turn your attention inward: how your voice sounds, where to put your hands, or what others are thinking. This self-examination intensifies the feeling of being under a spotlight.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
For the human brain, belonging and being accepted is very important. When you anticipate a social evaluation, your protective system may treat a look, a silence, or the possibility of making a mistake as signals of threat. The autonomic system increases activation: flushing, sweating, trembling, palpitations or a blank mind appear. These are real bodily responses, not evidence that you are making a fool of yourself.

Attention usually turns inward to monitor the voice, the hands, or each word. That self-examination takes up resources you would normally use to listen and respond, and makes you feel even more exposed. Furthermore, a mind preoccupied with rejection tends to complete ambiguous gestures with negative interpretations. Expectations can change your experience, but they don't let you know what another person thinks.

Bringing attention to the content of the conversation and choosing a small social action reduces the burden. Every tolerable experience in which you nervously participate and remain safe offers the brain corrective information. With gradual practice you can learn that anxiety is uncomfortable, but it doesn't always need to direct your behavior.
situations.reassurance: You can participate with nerves. Success in this moment is not about appearing perfectly calm, but about taking a manageable step.
redFlags: The situation includes harassment, threats, discrimination, or a person not respecting your boundaries.
You have new or severe physical symptoms that may require medical attention.
whenToSeekHelp: If you persistently avoid studying, working, eating or socializing due to social fear.
If you turn to alcohol or other substances to cope with encounters.
If the anguish is intense, it lasts for months or ideas of harming yourself appear.

protocols.title: Focus outside of you
protocols.summary: Reduce self-examination by bringing attention to real data in the conversation.
protocols.caution: Do not use the technique to remain in a harassing or dangerous situation. You can leave and ask for support.

steps.title: Support your feet
steps.instruction: Notice both feet and allow the exhale to come out without forcing it.
steps.accessibilityCue: Notice the support of your feet.

steps.title: Find three details
steps.instruction: Look at three neutral details in the room: a shape, a color, and a light source.
steps.accessibilityCue: Locate three neutral details in the environment.

steps.title: Listen to a phrase
steps.instruction: Choose to listen to a complete sentence from another person without yet preparing your response.
steps.accessibilityCue: Listen to a complete sentence.

steps.title: Ask a simple question
steps.instruction: Use a short, open question: how did it go? What do you think? What do you need now?
steps.accessibilityCue: Ask a short, open-ended question.

steps.title: Return to content
steps.instruction: When you notice self-examination, call it inward attention and return to what the person is saying.
steps.accessibilityCue: Go back to the content of the conversation.

protocols.title: First minute plan
protocols.summary: Turn the encounter into three small actions that don't depend on feeling safe.
protocols.caution: Start with a tolerable challenge. Exposing yourself suddenly to an overwhelming situation can be counterproductive.

steps.title: Define the minimum
steps.instruction: Choose a small goal: come in, say hello, or stay five minutes.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a small social goal.

steps.title: Prepare an opening
steps.instruction: Decide on a simple and natural phrase to start: Hello, how are you? or thanks for inviting me.
steps.accessibilityCue: Prepare a simple sentence to start.

steps.title: Prepare an exit
steps.instruction: Remember that you can say: I'm going to take a breath for a moment, I'll be right back.
steps.accessibilityCue: Have a respectful pause prepared.

steps.title: Just take the first step
steps.instruction: Take the first action of the plan without yet evaluating how the entire encounter will go.
steps.accessibilityCue: Only do the first action.

steps.title: Recognize the action
steps.instruction: Appreciate what you did, not if your nerves disappeared. Then decide the next step.
steps.accessibilityCue: Recognize the action you have completed.

protocols.title: Gentle voice warm-up
protocols.summary: Loosen your jaw and warm up your voice with a gentle hum before entering the conversation.
protocols.caution: The sound should be comfortable and low. Stop if it irritates your throat or makes you dizzy.

steps.accessibilityCue: Make a soft hum.

steps.title: say a phrase
steps.instruction: In a low voice, practice your greeting or first question without trying to make it sound perfect.
steps.accessibilityCue: Practice a short phrase.

practicalTips.detail: A glass, notebook or pen can give your hands a natural position.

practicalTips.title: arrive a little early
practicalTips.detail: Entering when the place is quiet can make it easier to get your bearings before the noise increases.

practicalTips.title: Prepare an exit sentence
practicalTips.detail: Knowing that you can say “I'm going to take a breath and come back” reduces the feeling of being trapped.

situations.title: A wave of grief has hit me
situations.subtitle: A loss or memory brings sadness, anger, emptiness or disbelief
situations.immediateExplanation: The duel does not follow a fixed order. A song, a date or a place can reactivate intense emotions even after a calmer period.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your brain and your body had learned to count on that link. The lost person, relationship, or reality was part of many everyday predictions: who to call, what to expect when you get home, or how to imagine the future. After loss, those models are not updated all at once. A song, a smell, or a date can trigger memories and a search response before you've consciously thought about it.

Grief involves attachment, attention, memory, stress, and reward systems; That's why it can feel like sadness, anger, emptiness, restlessness or even physical pain. Waves don't follow a set schedule, and a strong respawn doesn't mean you've gone backwards. Your body is trying to integrate a reality that matters deeply.

Allowing emotion while keeping an anchor in the present avoids adding a second battle against what you feel. New habits, supports, and meanings can help the brain build a life that includes the loss without erasing the connection or memories. This learning is gradual and does not require "closing" the grief. If pain threatens your safety or prevents you from sustaining basic needs, you deserve professional support.
situations.reassurance: You do not need to close or overcome the loss during this exercise. Now it is enough to go through this wave in a safe and accompanied way.
redFlags: You have thoughts of suicide, harming yourself, or feel like you can't keep yourself safe.
The loss has just occurred in a violent, traumatic context or with danger still present.
whenToSeekHelp: If the intensity persistently prevents taking care of basic needs or carrying out daily life.
If you have symptoms of traumatic stress, you use substances to cope with it or you isolate yourself completely.
If you need accompaniment: there is no need to wait until you are at your limit to ask for it.

protocols.title: Make room for the surge
protocols.summary: Recognize the emotion and keep part of your attention anchored in the present.
protocols.caution: If the memory becomes unbearable, intense disconnection appears, or you lose orientation, stop the exercise and seek company or professional help.

steps.title: Name the wave
steps.instruction: Complete: right now there is sadness, anger, fear, emptiness or whatever word best fits.
steps.accessibilityCue: Give a simple name to what you feel.

steps.title: Recognize the link

steps.title: keep an anchor
steps.instruction: Gently press your feet into the floor and look at a stable object in the present.
steps.accessibilityCue: Use your feet and an object as anchors to the present.

steps.title: Let a minute pass
steps.instruction: Allow tears or silence without analyzing the whole story. Observe how the intensity changes.
steps.accessibilityCue: Let the emotion be present for a moment.

steps.title: Choose basic care
steps.instruction: Decide on a small action: drink water, eat something, take a shower, or sit next to someone.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a basic care action.

protocols.summary: Transform immediate isolation into an acceptable contact or gesture of remembrance.
protocols.caution: Choose someone who can listen without pressuring you. You are under no obligation to share details you want to keep private.

steps.instruction: Think of someone safe who can accompany you without trying to fix everything.
steps.accessibilityCue: Think of a confident person.

steps.title: Formulate the request
steps.instruction: Prepare a concrete message: today I was hit by grief; can you listen to me for ten minutes?
steps.accessibilityCue: Prepare a specific request for company.

steps.instruction: Send the message or make the call. If they don't respond, try another person or support resource.
steps.accessibilityCue: Contact the chosen person.

steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a significant memory or quality.

steps.accessibilityCue: Calmly return to a concrete action in the present.

protocols.summary: A small rhythmic movement that accompanies the wave without demanding that it disappear.

steps.title: Maintain a link

practicalTips.detail: A photograph or object can give the memory a specific place during the wave.

practicalTips.title: Prepare something warm

situations.title: I just received some bad news
situations.subtitle: There is shock, confusion, or urgency to react immediately
situations.immediateExplanation: After shocking news, it is common to feel unreality, tremor, blockage or the need to act now. During the first minutes it can be difficult to organize information and prioritize.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Bad news suddenly breaks the model that your mind had of the next few minutes or the future. Faced with this unexpected change, the brain gives top priority to the information and activates stress responses. Adrenaline and other messengers increase alertness, the heart may race and the body may tremble. Some people feel an urgency to act; Others remain motionless, disconnected or with a feeling of unreality. They can all be initial responses to the impact.

During the peak, attention narrows and working memory retains less data. That's why you may need to listen to an explanation several times or not remember part of the conversation. The mind tries to fill in the gaps quickly and can jump from a confirmed fact to the worst imaginable future.

Sitting down, locating yourself and contacting someone provides signals of stability and reduces decisions. Separating facts, questions, and a single step restores structure to executive networks without asking you to understand everything. The presence of a safe person can also help regulate arousal. If the news involves current danger or a medical emergency, acting and contacting the appropriate services comes before any exercise.
situations.reassurance: You don't have to understand or decide everything now. First confirm security, then separate facts from uncertainties and look for company.
redFlags: The news involves current physical danger, a medical emergency, violence, or a missing person.
You are driving, operating machinery, or in a place where shock could put you at risk.
whenToSeekHelp: If you don't regain your bearings, you may faint, have chest pain, or have severe medical symptoms.
If thoughts of suicide or harm appear or you cannot guarantee your safety.
If nightmares, disconnection or marked inability to function persist in the following days.

protocols.title: First minutes
protocols.summary: Regain physical security and support before making important decisions.
protocols.caution: If there is a real emergency, call the corresponding service first. This guidance should not delay urgent care.

steps.title: Stop in a safe place

steps.accessibilityCue: Stop and find a safe position.

steps.title: Get your bearings
steps.instruction: Name where you are, what day it is and one thing you know for sure.

steps.accessibilityCue: Notice the physical support under your body.

steps.title: Contact

steps.accessibilityCue: Contact a safe person.

steps.title: Postpone the irreversible
steps.instruction: Unless security requires action, postpone public messages, purchases or irreversible decisions.
steps.accessibilityCue: Postpone irreversible decisions if they are not urgent.

protocols.title: Facts, doubts and next step
protocols.summary: Organize the information without trying to solve the entire future at once.
protocols.caution: Don't use this classification for compulsive research. If the information is medical, legal or security, confirm with the corresponding professional.

steps.title: Write the facts
steps.instruction: Write down only what is confirmed, with simple words and without interpretations.
steps.accessibilityCue: Write down only confirmed facts.

steps.title: Separate the unknown
steps.instruction: Make a short list of questions. Don't answer them with assumptions.
steps.accessibilityCue: Separate the questions that do not yet have answers.

steps.title: Identify what is urgent
steps.instruction: Question: Is there anything that needs to be done today for safety or actual deadline?
steps.accessibilityCue: Identify if there is a real urgency.

steps.title: Choose a font
steps.instruction: Decide who can confirm the following information: professional, responsible family member or official service.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a reliable source to confirm information.

steps.title: take a single step
steps.instruction: Make a call, take a note, or make an appointment. Then check back to see how you are doing.
steps.accessibilityCue: Only perform the next verifiable step.

protocols.title: Alternating touch and facts
protocols.summary: Combine gentle touches with brief repetition of what you know and what you don't know yet.

steps.title: Separate the doubt
steps.instruction: Stop the tapping and complete: “I don't know yet…” and “My next safe step is…”.
steps.accessibilityCue: Distinguish between doubt and the next step.

practicalTips.detail: Write down what they have communicated to you without interpretation so you can refer to it when memory fails.

practicalTips.title: Charge the phone

situations.title: Everything around me feels overwhelming
situations.subtitle: Noise, lights, people or simultaneous stimuli become unbearable
situations.immediateExplanation: When too many stimuli arrive at once it can be difficult to filter what deserves attention. Irritability, blockage or need to escape are signals to reduce load and recover margin.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Your brain continually receives much more sensory information than it can bring to consciousness. Normally filters, groups and prioritizes what is relevant. When there is fatigue, stress, pain or a particular sensitivity, this filtering may require more effort. Lights, voices, movement and contact compete at the same time, and what was previously background begins to feel intense or invasive.

If the brain interprets that it cannot organize or escape from that load, the autonomic response increases: irritability, tension, rapid breathing, blockage or an urgent need to get out appears. It is not a lack of will and the stimulus does not have to be dangerous to be physically overwhelming. The system is signaling that it has exceeded its current processing capacity.

Reducing a channel—brightness, sound, or social demand—reduces incoming information and allows margin to be recovered. Attending to a single sense helps organize the experience instead of fighting it all at once. Over time you can learn to recognize early signs and adjust your environment before it overwhelms. Environmental adaptation is regulation, not failure; If the sensitivity is sudden, painful or frequent, possible medical causes should be evaluated.
situations.reassurance: Moving away, dimming the lights or using hearing protection is not failure. It is adjusting the environment so that your system can recover capacity.
redFlags: The tenderness came on suddenly with weakness, slurred speech, disorientation, extreme headache, or loss of vision.
You are in a crowd, road or other place where you need to get out with help to do so safely.
whenToSeekHelp: If these episodes are new, frequent, or interfere with study, work, sleep, or self-care.
If you suspect migraine, medication effects, hearing loss or another medical cause.
If overload leads to self-harm, aggression or inability to keep yourself safe.

protocols.title: Reduce sensory input
protocols.summary: Reduce noise, light, physical contact, and social demands in an orderly way.
protocols.caution: Don't close your eyes or block out sounds if you need to monitor traffic, machinery, or other safety signs.

steps.title: Find the edge

steps.accessibilityCue: Go to a place with less stimuli.

steps.title: Reduce a channel

steps.title: Avoid new lawsuits
steps.instruction: Say if necessary: I need two minutes in silence and then I will respond.

steps.title: Find stability
steps.instruction: Look at a smooth surface or a stationary object and notice the support of your back or feet.
steps.accessibilityCue: Look at a stationary object and notice a support point.

steps.title: Decide on the following environment
steps.instruction: Choose to stay with adjustments, leave with someone, or return when there is less load.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose the most manageable environment to continue.

steps.accessibilityCue: Follow the outline of an object.

steps.title: Expand little by little
steps.instruction: Look around and decide if you can incorporate a task or if you need more time with low stimulation.

situations.title: I feel stuck and can't get started
situations.subtitle: A task feels too big, confusing, or unpleasant
situations.immediateExplanation: Blocking does not always mean lack of interest or ability. When a task seems ambiguous, enormous, or linked to the fear of failure, avoiding it offers immediate relief and makes it harder to approach later.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Starting a task requires several operations: maintaining the objective, deciding the first move, estimating effort and inhibiting distractions. When the task is ambiguous, huge, or linked to the fear of failure, your brain anticipates discomfort and cost before you have even started. Stress takes up some of your executive resources, and the goal of “getting it all done” does not provide a clear physical action to take.

Avoidance produces immediate relief. That short break works as learning: the brain registers that walking away reduces the discomfort and suggests repeating it the next time. It is not laziness or a completely conscious decision; It is a cycle of anticipation, avoidance and short-term reward that can become stronger.

Converting the project into “open the file” or “write a title” reduces uncertainty and the number of decisions. The action provides new evidence: starting out may be smaller than my prediction said. Each repetition helps associate the initial discomfort with a manageable movement, not with all the future effort. Neuroplasticity needs practice and realistic conditions; If the blockage is generalized or accompanied by very low morale, it deserves a broader assessment.
situations.reassurance: You don't need to finish or feel motivated. You just need to make the first move visible and possible.
redFlags: The block appears along with sudden confusion, weakness, slurred speech, or other new neurological symptoms.
You can't meet basic needs, get out of bed, or stay safe.
whenToSeekHelp: If the blockage is generalized, lasts weeks or significantly affects work, study, self-care or relationships.
If it is accompanied by very low mood, extreme exhaustion, intense anxiety or significant sleep changes.
If you suspect attention difficulties, depression or another condition that requires professional evaluation.

situations.title: Guilt or shame overwhelms me
situations.subtitle: A mistake becomes a judgment against your entire person
situations.immediateExplanation: Guilt can signal that a behavior clashed with your values; Shame usually broadens the judgment from I did something wrong to I am bad. Under a lot of activation, that difference is lost and concealment, attack or punishment appear.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Guilt and shame are related, but they don't do exactly the same job. Guilt usually points to behavior that clashed with your values: “I did something that I need to review.” Shame broadens the message to your entire identity: “there is something wrong with me.” Since belonging and acceptance are important, both can activate vigilance, tension, the desire to hide, or the impulse to defend yourself by attacking.

Your mind can review the mistake to avoid repeating it and recover social security. When new information no longer appears, this mechanism becomes rumination: it keeps the threat present, but does not repair the damage. Global labels also reduce options; If "I am unforgivable," it seems that no concrete action can change anything.

Describing the event, recognizing the impact and choosing a repair transforms a diffuse alarm into learning. Treating yourself humanely does not eliminate responsibility; It helps maintain enough regulation to take it on without destroying yourself. Repeating honesty, boundary, and repair responses can strengthen an identity based on chosen behaviors, not a single episode. If the guilt stems from abuse or leads you to want to physically punish yourself, seek safe support.
situations.reassurance: Taking responsibility and treating yourself humanely can coexist. Punishing yourself does not repair the damage by itself.
redFlags: Guilt comes from abuse, manipulation, blackmail, or someone holding you responsible for their violence.
You feel like you deserve to get hurt, disappear, or receive physical punishment.
whenToSeekHelp: If the guilt is persistent, disproportionate, or related to traumatic memories.
If you compulsively make verifications, confessions or requests for peace of mind.
If there are thoughts of self-harm, suicide or inability to keep yourself safe.

protocols.title: Facts vs verdict
protocols.summary: Distinguish specific behavior from absolute labels about who you are.
protocols.caution: Don't minimize real damage. The goal is to describe it accurately so you can respond responsibly.

steps.title: Write the fact

steps.accessibilityCue: Describe the event without labeling yourself.

steps.title: Detect the verdict

steps.accessibilityCue: Identify the global judgment about you.

steps.title: Add context without excusing
steps.instruction: Recognize what influenced it and what part was still under your responsibility.
steps.accessibilityCue: Separate the context from your responsibility.

steps.title: Identify the value
steps.instruction: Ask what value was violated: honesty, care, respect, commitment or other.
steps.accessibilityCue: Name the value you want to recover.

steps.title: Trade judgment for direction
steps.instruction: Formula: I did this, I care about this value and my next responsible action will be…
steps.accessibilityCue: Turn judgment into responsible direction.

protocols.title: Repair in three movements
protocols.summary: Prepare an apology or correction focused on the impact and possible change.
protocols.caution: Do not contact a person if there is an order, an explicit limit, or if doing so would put someone at risk. Repair by another appropriate means.

steps.title: Recognize
steps.instruction: Say what happened without if, but without an explanation that erases the impact.
steps.accessibilityCue: Clearly recognize what happened.

steps.title: Name the impact
steps.instruction: Mention the effect you know. If you don't know, don't make it up and ask when appropriate.
steps.accessibilityCue: Name the known impact without assuming.

steps.title: Propose repair
steps.instruction: Choose a specific correction that respects what the other person needs.
steps.accessibilityCue: Propose a concrete and respectful repair.

steps.title: Accept the limit
steps.instruction: Remember that apologizing does not require immediate forgiveness, response, or trust again.
steps.accessibilityCue: Accept that you do not control the other person's response.

steps.title: Change a condition
steps.instruction: Define what you will do differently to reduce the likelihood of repeating it.
steps.accessibilityCue: Decide on a concrete change for the future.

protocols.title: Self-compassion gesture
protocols.summary: Use careful contact and language to be able to look at the event without turning it into condemnation.
protocols.caution: If body contact is uncomfortable, rest your hands on a table or hold a neutral object.

steps.title: Choose a support
steps.instruction: Place one hand on your chest, forearm, or on a firm surface.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a comfortable support.

steps.title: Speak like someone else
steps.instruction: Say what happened in concrete words and add what you would say to someone you love who wanted to make amends.
steps.accessibilityCue: Use a fair and careful voice.

steps.title: Combine care and responsibility
steps.instruction: Complete: "I can treat myself with dignity and my next possible reparation is..."
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a possible repair.

practicalTips.detail: Describing a behavior keeps open the possibility of learning, correcting or repairing.

practicalTips.title: Imagine a fair witness
practicalTips.detail: Ask what a compassionate person who also values responsibility would say.

situations.title: I feel very alone or disconnected
situations.subtitle: You need closeness, but contacting someone seems too difficult
situations.immediateExplanation: Loneliness is an experience of perceived disconnection; It can appear even surrounded by people. Sometimes he pushes away just when a small sign of contact would be helpful.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
Human beings regulate part of our security and well-being in relation to other people. A familiar voice, an attentive response, or sharing a space can act as signals of support. When you perceive a lack of connection, the brain increases social vigilance: it looks for signs of rejection and can interpret a late message or an ambiguous gesture in the most painful way. Loneliness can be felt even in company because it depends on the connection you need, not just the number of people around you.

That vigilance may push you to withdraw to avoid another rejection. Isolation reduces opportunities to receive different signals and confirms the feeling of being alone. It is not a voluntary contradiction, but an attempt at protection that ends up maintaining the problem.

A secure microconnection provides new information with little demand. Conversation, shared presence, and community routines can facilitate coregulation: each person still has his or her own nervous system, but the tone, predictability, and availability of another helps reduce alertness. Repeating sufficiently secure contacts allows trust to be gradually rebuilt. You don't need to return to an unhealthy relationship to meet this need.
situations.reassurance: Needing connection is not a weakness. You don't have to have a perfect conversation to create a first point of contact.
redFlags: Loneliness comes with thoughts of suicide, self-harm, or the feeling that no one can stop you.
You are isolated because of control, threats, violence, or because another person prevents you from asking for help.
whenToSeekHelp: If isolation is prolonged, it worsens your health or prevents you from carrying out basic activities.
If anxiety, depression, grief or other difficulty makes it impossible to maintain relationships.
If you need urgent support: use emergency resources even if it is difficult for you to explain everything.

protocols.caution: Choose a public and safe space. If going out is not possible, use moderate online community activity and protect your personal data.

steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a safe place with the presence of other people.

steps.title: Define a short stay

steps.accessibilityCue: Defines a brief and undemanding stay.

steps.title: Carry out a simple activity

steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a simple activity to accompany the outing.

steps.title: Recognize humanity

steps.accessibilityCue: Observe neutral signs of human activity.

steps.title: Decide on next contact

protocols.title: Warmth and a human voice
protocols.summary: Combine safe warmth with the sound of a human voice to ease the immediate sense of emptiness.
protocols.caution: Avoid very hot objects and do not use audio if sadness or overload increases.

steps.title: Seek safe warmth
steps.instruction: Hold a warm cup or wrap yourself in a blanket, making sure the temperature is comfortable.
steps.accessibilityCue: Find a comfortable temperature.

steps.title: Add a voice
steps.instruction: Play a familiar voice, calm radio or message from someone safe at low volume.
steps.accessibilityCue: Hear a calm voice.

steps.title: make a bridge
steps.instruction: Send a brief greeting or decide on a place with human presence that you can approach.
steps.accessibilityCue: Create a small bridge to another person.

practicalTips.detail: A quiet radio, podcast, or broadcast can make the silence less abrupt.

situations.title: Jealousy or insecurity is taking control
situations.subtitle: An ambiguous signal activates fear, comparison, and the urge to check.
situations.immediateExplanation: Jealousy can mix fear of losing a connection, comparison, anger and desire for certainty. The urge to review, accuse, or demand can alleviate doubt for a few seconds and increase conflict later.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
When an important bond seems threatened, your attachment and protection system increases vigilance. Attention looks for changes in messages, gestures or availability, and the body can activate tension, heat, palpitations or urgency to check. Uncertainty is especially uncomfortable because the brain wants to predict whether it will maintain a relationship that it considers valuable.

With a lot of activation, the gaps quickly fill with stories built from fears and previous experiences. Then a confirmation bias appears: signals that fit the suspicion attract more attention than those that contradict it. This doesn't mean that jealousy is always unfounded or that you should ignore a real breach of agreements; It means that emotion, data and interpretation are not the same thing.

Stopping the check allows the urgency to go down and separate "I saw this" from "I'm afraid it means this." Formulating the need—clarity, respect, affection, or a boundary—puts options back into the conversation. Practicing this sequence teaches the brain that it can seek safety through information and boundaries, not control. If there is violence, surveillance or fear, the priority is not to better regulate jealousy, but to protect the people involved.
situations.reassurance: An intense emotion does not prove that your interpretation is true or force you to act. You can protect your boundaries without controlling another person.
redFlags: There is violence, threats, coercive control, following, fear or destruction of objects.
You feel the urge to attack, chase, access other people's devices or prevent someone from leaving.
whenToSeekHelp: Whether jealousy leads to surveillance, interrogations, isolation or repeated conflicts.
If there is a betrayal or real problem that needs couple support or individual counseling.
If you fear harm or harm, stay away and use emergency help or violence resources in your country.

protocols.title: Fact, story, and need
protocols.summary: Separate what you observed from what your mind predicts before acting.
protocols.caution: Separating interpretations does not mean ignoring facts of deception, abuse or breach of agreements. Seek information and safe limits.

steps.title: Stop checking
steps.instruction: During this exercise, do not check messages, networks, locations or devices.
steps.accessibilityCue: Pause any check.

steps.title: Write the data
steps.instruction: Describe only what you saw or heard, without guessing intent or meaning.
steps.accessibilityCue: It only describes the observed data.

steps.title: Name the story
steps.instruction: Complete: my mind is telling that... It includes the worst outcome it anticipates.
steps.accessibilityCue: Name the interpretation as a story of your mind.

steps.title: Identify the need
steps.instruction: Ask if you need clarity, respect, consistency, affection, an agreement or a boundary.
steps.accessibilityCue: Identify the need underlying jealousy.

steps.title: Choose compatible behavior
steps.instruction: Decide on a respectful question, pause, or boundary that isn't invasive or threatening.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose behavior that is respectful and compatible with your values.

protocols.title: Conversation without accusation
protocols.summary: Prepare a message about observation, emotion, need and specific request.
protocols.caution: Do not start the conversation if someone is intoxicated, driving, shouting, or preventing you from leaving. Wait or seek support.

steps.title: Check intensity
steps.instruction: If you can't speak without insulting, threatening, or questioning, take a longer pause first.
steps.accessibilityCue: See if you can talk without escalating the conflict.

steps.title: Start with observation
steps.instruction: Formula: when it happened... and use a specific fact, without always or never.
steps.accessibilityCue: Start with a concrete observation.

steps.title: Speak from you
steps.instruction: Add: I felt... Avoid turning emotion into an accusation.
steps.accessibilityCue: Name your emotion without accusing.

steps.title: Make a request
steps.instruction: Ask for an observable action or conversation: can we clarify...? or do we agree...?
steps.accessibilityCue: Formulate a clear and negotiable request.

steps.title: Leave space for response
steps.instruction: Listen to the full response and remember that a request can be negotiated or rejected.
steps.accessibilityCue: Listen and leave room for a real response.

protocols.title: Hand self-massage
protocols.summary: Give your hands a slow task while you separate the urge to check or accuse.
protocols.caution: The pressure should be comfortable. Avoid inflamed, injured areas or areas with loss of sensitivity.

steps.title: open your hands
steps.instruction: Support your forearms and see if you are gripping the phone or tensing your fingers.
steps.accessibilityCue: Drop whatever you have in your hands.

steps.title: Massage
steps.instruction: With your thumb, slowly run over the opposite palm and then change hands.
steps.accessibilityCue: Massage your palms gently.

steps.title: Postpone the check
steps.instruction: Put the phone face down and decide how long you will wait before asking or checking.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a waiting time.

practicalTips.title: Put the phone away
practicalTips.detail: Leave it out of reach for a few minutes so you don't turn an emotion into impulsive vigilance.

practicalTips.title: Write three possible explanations
practicalTips.detail: Include at least a neutral interpretation of the same data, even if it still doesn't convince you.

practicalTips.title: Use an object as a reminder
practicalTips.detail: A bracelet or coin can mean: “I ask first; "I neither divine nor accuse."

situations.title: I feel an urge I might regret
situations.subtitle: You want to send, buy, consume, break or act without thinking
situations.immediateExplanation: An intense impulse creates a sense of urgency and narrows the options to act or resist. Between the two there is a third way: delay, create distance and observe how it changes before deciding.
situations.biologicalExplanation:
An impulse is an intense preparation to act, not an inevitable order. Threat, emotion, and reward networks can mark a behavior as urgent and bring all your attention to its immediate relief. Dopaminergic signals participate in the importance and learning associated with certain options; They are not a “pleasure chemical” that alone controls your decisions. Context, habits, and learned consequences also play a role.

With stress, intoxication or lack of sleep, inhibitory control usually works worse and it is difficult to maintain the consequences of today, tomorrow and next month at the same time. The mind reduces the world to "do it or endure it", even though there are more alternatives. The intensity of the impulse usually rises, fluctuates and falls, but does not follow an exact clock.

Delaying and physical distancing add friction when thinking is not enough. This time allows some of the activation to decrease and the executive networks to once again represent consequences and options. Observing the sensation without obeying it practices an important learning: I can feel urgency and choose safety. If the impulse involves harm, overdose, weapons, or dangerous driving, don't wait for it to pass on its own; Stay away from the media and activate immediate help.
situations.reassurance: Feeling an impulse is not the same as choosing it. You can postpone the decision and make the safe option the easiest for the next few minutes.
redFlags: The impulse involves suicide, self-harm, overdose, assaulting someone, using a weapon, driving dangerously, or starting a fire.
You've already taken a substance, started a dangerous action, or don't trust yourself to stop.
whenToSeekHelp: If there is any immediate risk, stay away from the media, find another person and contact emergencies or a crisis line in your country.
If the impulses are repeated, they generate debt, consumption, injuries or damage to relationships.
If they appear with extreme mood swings, very little sleep or intoxication.

protocols.title: Delay and distance
protocols.summary: Add time and concrete obstacles between impulse and action.
protocols.caution: Do not use this guide as the only response to impulses to harm yourself or someone. In that case activate immediate help and do not be left alone.

steps.title: Declare a delay
steps.instruction: Say: I won't decide this for the next ten minutes. Postponing does not mean denying forever.
steps.accessibilityCue: Postpone the decision for ten minutes.

steps.title: Create physical distance
steps.instruction: Leave the object, device, card, substance or keys out of reach and change spaces.
steps.accessibilityCue: Put distance between you and the means of acting.

steps.title: Add a barrier
steps.instruction: Close the app, temporarily block the purchase, or give the media to a safe person.
steps.accessibilityCue: It adds a practical barrier to impulsive action.

steps.title: inform someone
steps.instruction: Say clearly: I have a strong urge and I need you to stay with me while the peak passes.
steps.accessibilityCue: Ask for company while the urgency subsides.

steps.title: Check consequences
steps.instruction: When the delay is over, compare what happens if you act today, tomorrow, and a month from now. If it is still dangerous, maintain the barrier and seek help.
steps.accessibilityCue: Review consequences before deciding again.

protocols.title: Observe the urge wave
protocols.summary: Locate the urge in the body and observe its changes without obeying it.
protocols.caution: Don't close your eyes if you need to monitor your safety. If the urge is dangerous or increases, stop the exercise and contact immediate help.

steps.title: Rate the urgency
steps.instruction: Rate its intensity from zero to ten without trying to obtain an exact figure.
steps.accessibilityCue: Evaluate the approximate intensity of the impulse.

steps.title: Locate it
steps.instruction: Note where it manifests itself: hands, jaw, chest, abdomen, legs or another area.
steps.accessibilityCue: Locate the sensations of impulse in the body.

steps.title: Describe, don't order
steps.instruction: Use sensory words like pressure, heat, movement or tension, without saying I have to.
steps.accessibilityCue: Describe the feeling without turning it into an order.

steps.title: Observe the change
steps.instruction: For a minute, see if the shape, location, or intensity changes, even a little.
steps.accessibilityCue: Observe how the sensation changes for a minute.

steps.title: Choose the safe action
steps.instruction: Score again and make an alternative incompatible with the impulse: walk away, call, walk with someone, or maintain the barrier.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose a safe action incompatible with impulse.

protocols.title: Cool water on face and hands
protocols.summary: A brief sensory change to create distance before acting, without using extreme cold.
protocols.caution: Use cool water, not ice; do not submerge your face or hold your breath. Avoid if cold worsens a medical condition.

steps.title: Create distance
steps.instruction: Leave the object, application, or place related to the impulse and go to a safe sink.
steps.accessibilityCue: Move away from the middle of the momentum.

steps.title: Use fresh water
steps.instruction: Run cool water over your hands and, if comfortable, gently splash it on your cheeks.
steps.accessibilityCue: Feel fresh water on your hands and face.

steps.title: Maintain the barrier
steps.instruction: Dry yourself slowly and choose an incompatible action: calling, walking with someone, or temporarily blocking access.
steps.accessibilityCue: Choose an incompatible safe action.

practicalTips.title: Add a real obstacle
practicalTips.detail: Hand over keys or cards, sign out, or move the item to a hard-to-reach location.

practicalTips.detail: Mint or an acidic food can disrupt autopilot; avoid allergies and risks when swallowing.

practicalTips.title: Submit a keyword
practicalTips.detail: Agree with someone on a word that means "I need company without explaining everything right now."
